name: Tekal Agua de Jamaica Reserve
description: A premium carbonated hibiscus drink using real dried hibiscus flowers sourced from licensed equatorial grow operations. Tekal is explicit about its sourcing and publishes full supply chain transparency reports quarterly — an unusual practice that has become part of its brand identity.
flavor_profile: Deep, tart hibiscus with a clean cranberry-like acidity; real-extract complexity with floral depth, moderate sweetness, long dry finish with subtle earthiness
slogan: You know where it comes from.
cultural_context: Tekal occupies a specific cultural position: it is the beverage of people who care about supply chains, labor conditions, and what 'real' means in a world of synth-everything. It's drunk at activist meetings, co-op dinners, and community governance assemblies. It's also drunk by Tier 4 consumers who want ethical credentials without lifestyle disruption. The two groups don't always acknowledge each other across the same can.
story_hooks: Tekal's published supply chain report contains a discrepancy that a careful reader has flagged — one of their grow operations lists a labor certification that doesn't match public records. Tekal's transparency is either imperfect or deliberately constructed to look transparent while concealing something specific.

A corponation has made an acquisition offer for Tekal. The founder wants to refuse. The board is split. The activist community that built Tekal's reputation is watching and has made clear that a sale would be treated as a betrayal — with consequences.

The equatorial grow operation supplying Tekal's hibiscus is in a region experiencing escalating resource conflict. The farmers have reached out to Tekal for support. Tekal's response — or lack of one — will define what their transparency branding actually means.
